A product page gets its prices from an internal pricing API that takes about 200 ms per call, so the team caches each price for five minutes with

. The hit rate looks excellent. Yet the pricing team keeps reporting the same pattern: every few minutes, a wall of identical requests for the most popular products, and after each deploy, enough of them to hit the API's rate limit. The cache is working. It just isn't doing the one thing everyone assumed it does.
runs the factory once per key. Concurrent requests for a missing key wait for the first one to fill it, and the cache takes care of the rest, even across several server instances.
The name does most of the convincing: "get or create" sounds like a single step. The docs say
is thread-safe, which is true and easy to over-read. And in development, with one request at a time, the factory really does run once per expiration.
But thread-safe means the cache's own data structure won't be corrupted. It says nothing about the code you pass in.

is an extension method that looks up the key and, on a miss, runs your factory and stores the result. Nothing stops other callers between the lookup and the store. The memory cache docs say it directly: these methods aren't atomic, each request that misses runs the factory, and the last value written is the one that stays. Tested on .NET 10: 100 concurrent callers on a cold key with a 200 ms factory produced 100 factory calls.
Every expiry opens the window again
That burst isn't a one-time startup cost. Each time a popular entry expires, every request that arrives before the new value is stored runs the factory. That's a
. Every deploy, restart and scale-out starts with an empty cache and repeats it. And
lives inside one process, so five servers mean five separate caches, five separate stampedes, and possibly five different values for the same key.
package, changes the first part. Within one

instance, only one concurrent caller per key runs the factory; the others wait for its result. In the same test, 100 concurrent callers produced one factory call. When the factory threw, all 20 waiting callers received the exception, nothing was cached, and the next call ran the factory again.
keeps entries in process memory first. If the app registers an out-of-process

, such as Redis, it becomes the second level: values found there skip the factory, and new values are written to both. In a test with two instances sharing a second level, a cold key called the factory twice, once per instance. A third instance started later read the value from the shared level and didn't call it at all.
